claim: Replace emoji used as UI iconography with glyphs from a single interface icon library (Phosphor, Lucide, or equivalent) so weight, grid, and stroke stay consistent across the product.
why: Emoji render differently per platform, carry their own colours and illustrative style, and cannot be tuned to match a UI's stroke weight or colour — so they read as filler rather than as a designed system.
when: Any product chrome: card headers, nav items, list rows, buttons, empty states.
fails: Products that adopt emoji deliberately and consistently as part of their identity — user-chosen page icons, reactions, tagging — where the emoji is content the user picked, not an interface affordance.

claim: Do not ship a colour palette an AI generated for you; pick the hues yourself and treat the generated one as a placeholder.
why: Models default to high-saturation hues chosen individually rather than as a related set, so the result has no coherent relationship between surface, accent, and data colours.
when: Any AI-scaffolded interface being taken toward production.

claim: Fix a broken palette by changing the base surface hue first, before touching accents — one substitution at the background level re-tunes everything sitting on it.
why: Every foreground colour is read relative to the surface behind it, so the background is the highest-leverage single change and avoids re-picking every accent by hand.
when: Restyling an existing screen whose colours feel off but whose layout is roughly sound.

claim: Let data carry the colour in a dashboard: strip decorative icons from KPI tiles and put charts in their place rather than adding coloured buttons or badges.
why: Colour attached to real values is informative and earns its salience; colour attached to ornament competes with the data for attention and adds nothing.
when: Dashboards, analytics views, and any metric-dense surface.

claim: Pair every headline KPI number with a micro chart (sparkline or small bar series) showing its recent trajectory.
why: A bare number states a level but not a direction; the trend is usually the thing the viewer actually wants and it costs very little space.
when: KPI tiles at the top of a dashboard where historical data exists.

claim: Give KPI tiles more room when you upgrade them — expand the tile footprint rather than compressing a chart into the space an icon used to occupy.
why: Trend visuals need horizontal extent to be legible; squeezing them into leftover ornament space produces an unreadable smear.
when: Converting icon-decorated stat cards into data-bearing cards.

claim: Judge a redesign by whether the after-state conveys more information than the before-state, not by whether it looks cleaner.
why: Prettiness is easy to reach by deletion alone; the standard that matters is whether the same pixel area now answers more of the user's questions.
when: Reviewing any visual overhaul of an existing screen.

claim: Audit an AI-built screen for repeated blocks — the same component appearing multiple times on one page is a generation artefact, not a considered layout.
why: Models pad a page by duplicating whatever component they already produced, the visual equivalent of stylistic tics in generated prose.
when: First pass over any scaffolded page before manual design work.

claim: Do not display per-item metrics (counts, badges, secondary stats) on navigation items; put those numbers on the dashboard or analytics surface where the user goes to actually read data.
why: Navigation is used to get somewhere, not to consume analytics. Metrics attached to nav links compete with the labels for attention and are ignored in the moment the user is navigating.
when: Sidebar or top-level nav in a product where per-section stats exist and could technically be surfaced
fails: The count is the reason to click — an unread/pending/error count that drives an action (inbox, approvals queue) belongs in the nav

claim: Left-align sidebar navigation labels and icons on a shared vertical axis, and reduce vertical spacing so the item list reads as one group rather than scattered rows.
why: A single left edge gives the eye one scan line down the list; tight spacing signals that the items belong to the same set.
when: Vertical nav lists of related destinations
fails: Deliberate spacing breaks are needed to separate distinct nav groups from each other

claim: Replace the gradient circle containing a user's initials with a real account card showing name, plan or workspace, and a clear affordance to open account actions.
why: The auto-generated gradient monogram is a generator default that carries no product information; an account card uses the same space to convey identity and state.
when: The account/profile block in a sidebar or app shell
fails: Space-constrained chrome (collapsed sidebar, top bar) where only an avatar-sized target fits

claim: Collapse a cluster of secondary account links into a popover opened by clicking the account block, rather than listing each one permanently in the sidebar.
why: Secondary destinations are visited rarely; permanently rendering them inflates the sidebar and dilutes the primary navigation.
when: Account, profile, help, or workspace-level links that are used occasionally
fails: Destinations used many times per session — hiding those behind a click adds friction on the hot path

claim: Group closely related settings destinations (e.g. settings, billing, usage) under a single parent entry instead of giving each its own top-level nav slot.
why: Related items consume one slot of the user's attention when grouped, and the shared parent is a more memorable target than three near-synonymous labels.
when: Nav lists where several items belong to the same conceptual area
fails: One of the grouped items is a primary, high-traffic destination in its own right

claim: When a list card looks busy, reduce it by demoting rather than deleting: move action buttons into an overflow (triple-dot) menu, strip chip labels down to icons, and keep only the primary metric as text.
why: Every persistent control on a repeated card multiplies across the list; demoting them preserves the capability while cutting the per-row visual weight.
when: Repeated cards or rows in a list view with multiple actions and status indicators
fails: The action is the main thing users do on that card — burying a primary action behind an overflow menu costs a click on every use; icon-only chips also fail when the icon set is not self-evident

claim: Give each element on a repeated card a fixed horizontal position and alignment — identity left, timestamp centred, metric right — so the same information sits at the same x-position in every row.
why: Consistent column positions let the eye scan down a single attribute across the list instead of re-reading each card's internal layout.
when: Lists of structurally identical cards or rows
fails: Cards with genuinely variable content shapes, where forced columns create large empty gaps

claim: Match the container to the form's content: use a modal for a form with few fields, and reserve side flyouts for content that benefits from vertical length or from keeping the underlying page visible.
why: A tall side panel holding three or four fields leaves large dead space and makes the task feel unfinished; a modal sizes to the content and centres the user's focus on a short, self-contained task.
when: Choosing the surface for a create/edit form in a web app
fails: The user needs to reference or interact with the list behind the form, or the form is long and benefits from a scrollable panel

claim: Treat AI-generated code as a reliable source of logic and behaviour but not of layout: specify the interaction rules to the generator, then re-decide the visual arrangement, hierarchy, and container choices yourself.
why: Generators reproduce common structural patterns and produce workable behaviour, but they have no model of which information matters most in this product, so their layouts default to uniform, undifferentiated density.
when: Any AI-assisted UI build

claim: Start AI UI generation with a small set of visual references and a specific design prompt, then plan to bring the output into an editable design tool.
why: References constrain the desired visual direction, while a precise prompt gives the model instructions it can act on.
when: You need a rapid first-pass UI design and intend to refine it visually afterward.
fails: null

claim: Provide a visual reference alongside a concise prompt when asking an AI model to generate a UI in a particular visual style.
why: The reference gives the model concrete stylistic direction beyond a text-only request.
when: You need an AI-generated interface to resemble a known aesthetic or design direction.
fails: The reference conflicts with the written requirements or does not clearly represent the intended style.

claim: Treat AI-generated UI as an editable first draft: preserve its useful layout, interaction, and responsive ideas, then refine visual details in a design tool.
why: The generated result can be strong overall while still containing taste-level mistakes such as overly frequent decorative elements.
when: An AI output is structurally useful but needs designer judgment and polish.

claim: Use decorative emojis sparingly and remove or replace them when they distract from a professional interface.
why: Overuse can make an otherwise appealing layout feel less controlled or less aligned with the desired tone.
when: Designing polished product interfaces with icons, labels, or status markers.
fails: A playful, emoji-native brand voice intentionally calls for dense emoji use.

claim: Provide a reference image when prompting an AI to create an interface with a specific visual style.
why: A visual example gives the AI a concrete target aesthetic beyond a text description.
when: The desired UI has a recognizable look, such as a dashboard or product-app style.

claim: Choose references with a clear, legible hierarchy rather than dense galleries full of small decorative details.
why: The AI may miss fine-grained visual cues in busy images and fail to extract the intended design direction.
when: Selecting screenshots or inspiration images to upload to an AI interface generator.
fails: When the detailed elements themselves are essential requirements and can be separately specified in the prompt.

claim: Use screenshots of real, production-like products as references when designing realistic application interfaces.
why: Real product UI tends to provide coherent, usable visual patterns instead of purely attention-grabbing presentation shots.
when: Creating practical dashboards, management tools, or SaaS interfaces.

claim: A reference image may come from your own mockup or an external inspiration source, as long as it communicates the intended direction clearly.
why: The useful input is the visual signal, not who created the image.
when: You need a style reference but do not already have a custom design file.

claim: When rapidly prototyping a polished interface, start from a curated component library and reuse either its code or its component prompt instead of rebuilding common patterns from scratch.
why: Prebuilt components package visual decisions and implementation details, reducing the work required to reach a refined result.
when: You are building a web UI and can adapt an existing component to the product’s visual system and technical stack.
fails: The component conflicts with accessibility, brand requirements, framework constraints, or the product’s interaction needs.

claim: Use a component’s full prompt as context for an AI coding assistant when you want the assistant to recreate or adapt that component in your project.
why: The prompt conveys the intended structure and styling instructions without requiring manual translation into a new request.
when: An AI assistant can accept a substantial prompt and generate code in a compatible frontend environment.
fails: The prompt lacks project-specific constraints such as framework, design tokens, dependencies, responsiveness, or accessibility requirements.

claim: Treat generated frontend code as a development artifact rather than a Figma-editable design file.
why: Code-oriented component formats do not directly map to Figma’s native editable document format.
when: Your workflow moves from an AI coding assistant into implementation.
fails: You use a separate conversion, recreation, or design-to-code workflow that specifically supports Figma interoperability.

claim: Open an AI UI prompt with an explicit instruction to design an interface, rather than assuming the model will infer the task.
why: A model can misclassify an underspecified request and produce something other than a design.
when: Prompting a general-purpose AI from a reference image or sparse brief.

claim: Request HTML and CSS output when the generated interface needs to be exported or reconstructed in Figma.
why: Structured web markup and styling provide a more transferable representation for that workflow.
when: The UI generation is intended to feed a Figma-oriented design process.

claim: Describe the product purpose and the user outcomes before listing visual details.
why: Functional context helps the model choose an interface structure that supports the actual workflow rather than creating a generic screen.
when: Creating an application UI, especially dashboards or task-oriented products.

claim: Name any essential UI regions, data visualizations, and distinctive properties directly in the prompt.
why: Explicit component requirements reduce the chance that important elements are omitted or interpreted generically.
when: The design requires particular elements such as navigation, sidebars, charts, or status displays.
fails: When prescribing every detail would prevent useful exploration or conflict with a simpler product need.

claim: Require a UI icon library for interface symbols instead of leaving icon treatment unspecified.
why: Without that constraint, the generated design may substitute emojis, which weakens a professional product UI aesthetic.
when: Designing app navigation, actions, and controls that need consistent symbolic icons.
fails: When an intentionally playful or conversational interface calls for emoji.

claim: Use AI-generated HTML as a fast structural starting point, then refine exact alignment, sticky behavior, and other small visual details in a design tool.
why: The generated result is usable and responsive but does not reliably reproduce fine-grained design details.
when: You need to turn an interface concept into an editable first pass quickly.
fails: Pixel-perfect reproduction of a highly detailed reference is required directly from the AI output.

claim: Do not rely on a single screenshot or visual-reference prompt to reproduce intricate UI details; inspect the result for omissions before treating it as final.
why: The comparison indicates that the model drops small details instead of accurately recreating them.
when: Rebuilding an existing polished interface from a Dribbble-style image or other raster reference.
fails: The desired outcome intentionally favors simplified structure over visual fidelity.

claim: Import exported HTML into Figma instead of importing a screenshot when you need editable, correctly structured interface elements.
why: HTML carries element structure, avoiding the artifacting and incorrect fragments associated with image-based conversion.
when: A working HTML implementation needs to become a Figma file for handoff or visual adjustment.
fails: Only a static visual reference is available and no editable HTML exists.

claim: During HTML-to-Figma import, keep the standard conversion settings but enable component generation and hover effects.
why: This preserves reusable UI structure and interactive states in the Figma result.
when: Converting an interface that contains repeatable controls or hover interactions.
fails: The source has no interactive states or the import plugin does not support those options.

claim: Prioritize font choice, alignment, and colour-system adjustments when polishing an AI-generated interface.
why: These changes create the largest visible improvement with relatively little editing effort.
when: A generated UI is structurally usable but feels generic, unbalanced, or visually inconsistent.

claim: Place account identity and account-switching controls together in the navigation area, using a name, avatar, and directional affordance.
why: Users can more readily recognize the active account and discover how to change it.
when: A product supports user profiles or multiple accounts.
fails: There is no account context to switch or display.

claim: Align navigation controls to a consistent edge and remove redundant category labels; place lower-priority actions such as settings and help at the bottom of the sidebar.
why: A cleaner hierarchy makes primary navigation easier to scan and separates routine destination links from utility actions.
when: Designing a persistent sidebar or vertical menu with both navigation and utility links.
fails: Settings or support are core workflow destinations that need equal prominence.

claim: Treat generated colours as a starting point and deliberately tune hue, darkness, and neutral balance to match the intended product mood.
why: A coherent palette can make the interface feel more purposeful even when the original colours are technically acceptable.
when: The initial UI palette feels off-brand or has an unwanted temperature or saturation bias.

claim: Verify contrast for compact status elements such as chips, not only for large text and backgrounds.
why: Small UI components can become hard to read or distinguish despite an otherwise acceptable palette.
when: Using coloured chips, badges, pills, or other dense status controls.

claim: Map visual state colours consistently: incomplete items must not use the same colour as completed items.
why: Reusing a completion colour for unfinished content gives users contradictory status signals.
when: A dashboard uses colour to communicate progress, completion, or task state.
fails: The repeated colour represents a different clearly labelled attribute.

claim: Use a numeric percentage for progress when a vague status label does not communicate the amount of completion.
why: A percentage gives the user an interpretable measure of progress.
when: A progress indicator needs to communicate how far a task or process has advanced.
fails: Progress is intentionally indeterminate or cannot be measured reliably.

claim: Add decorative background texture sparingly so it enriches the interface without competing with content.
why: A subtle pattern can add polish and depth while preserving hierarchy.
when: A dark or minimal interface has large quiet background areas.
fails: The texture lowers legibility or introduces visual noise.
